coredata.dc:description: In this study, spirobisindane-functionalized graphene oxide (SFGO)/polyimide (Matrimid® 5218, i.e. M) solutions are spin-coated onto a polysulfone support to produce SFGO@M nanocomposite membranes for alcohol dehydration by pervaporation. Compounds 3,3,3′,3′-tetramethyl-1,1′-spirobisindane-6,6′-diol (TSD) and 4,4′-((3,3,3′,3′-tetramethyl-2,2′,3,3′-tetrahydro-1,1′-spirobi[indene]-6,6′-diyl)bis(oxy))dianiline (TTSD) are synthesized based on a conversion reaction from bisphenol A (BPA). Both TSD and TTSD contain spirobisindane structure, which is inspired by the structural unit from polymers of intrinsic microporosity. The fine structural characteristics of SFGO@M membranes are evaluated using positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy. The membrane free volume increases in the following order: M < GO@M < BPA-GO@M < TSD-GO@M < TTSD-GO@M. These results reveal that SFGO affected the fine structural characteristics of membranes in a more significant manner when compared with GO@M and BPA-GO@M. Moreover, TSD-GO@M and TTSD-GO@M exhibit different levels of dehydration performance when tested on different alcohol feed solutions. After TTSD modification on GO, the membrane performance increased from 619.3 ± 124.0 g∙m-2h−1 for the pristine sample, to 915.5 ± 44.8 g∙m-2h−1 for TTSD-GO@M, and the water concentration in the permeate is maintained as high as 99 wt%. Furthermore, the modified membranes are stable under broad operating conditions with high potential for long-term use.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: In this study, spirobisindane-functionalized graphene oxide (SFGO)/polyimide (Matrimid® 5218, i.e. M) solutions are spin-coated onto a polysulfone support to produce SFGO@M nanocomposite membranes for alcohol dehydration by pervaporation. Both TSD and TTSD contain spirobisindane structure, which is inspired by the structural unit from polymers of intrinsic microporosity. The fine structural characteristics of SFGO@M membranes are evaluated using positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy. The membrane free volume increases in the following order: M < GO@M < BPA-GO@M < TSD-GO@M < TTSD-GO@M. These results reveal that SFGO affected the fine structural characteristics of membranes in a more significant manner when compared with GO@M and BPA-GO@M. Moreover, TSD-GO@M and TTSD-GO@M exhibit different levels of dehydration performance when tested on different alcohol feed solutions. After TTSD modification on GO, the membrane performance increased from 619.3 ± 124.0 g∙m-2h−1 for the pristine sample, to 915.5 ± 44.8 g∙m-2h−1 for TTSD-GO@M, and the water concentration in the permeate is maintained as high as 99 wt%. Furthermore, the modified membranes are stable under broad operating conditions with high potential for long-term use.

ce:section.ce:para: With the rapid development of industries, there is an increasing demand for petroleum and petrochemical energy. This causes the depletion of energy resources and destruction of the environment. Therefore, sustainable development has become a research priority throughout the world. Biofuels, when chosen as an alternative to fossil fuels, would decrease CO2 emissions in the transportation sector [1]. Biofuels can be produced from sugarcane, corn, wheat, and other classic agricultural food crops [2] through the processes of hydrolysis and fermentation. Acetone, n-butanol and ethanol mixture, or isopropanol, n-butanol and ethanol mixtures are produced during fermentation [3]. However, a large amount of water is used in the production of biofuels, where water is usually blended with alcohols. Therefore, the separation of alcohols/water is required.

Traditional distillation requires a lot of energy for the separation of water and alcohol from the solutions. Therefore, the distillation process should be replaced with a more sustainable approach to conserve energy. Pervaporation, a membrane separation process, requires lower energy than distillation [4]. It is sustainable because of the lesser greenhouse gases it emits to the environment. Another advantage of pervaporation over distillation includes the separation of azeotropic mixtures, thermally sensitive compounds, close-boiling point mixtures, and molecules that are similar in shape or weight [5]. Pervaporation membranes can be hydrophilic or organophilic. Hydrophilic polymers such as polyvinyl alcohol [6–8], chitosan [9–11], and sodium alginate [12–14] are preferred for dehydration of alcohols [15]. However, these polymers are easily swollen by water and polar solvents, especially at high temperatures, resulting in decreased stability [16,17]. Furthermore, the performance of many commercial pervaporation membranes used in processes decline in time due to poor thermal stability and mechanical properties. On the other hand, inorganic membranes can overcome swelling problems due to their high mechanical properties and excellent chemical and thermal resistance. However, inorganic membranes are not only more expensive than the polymeric membranes, but are also difficult to fabricate [18]. Hence, researchers have proposed other options such as increasing the stability of polymers by modification or using high performance polymers with high chemical and thermal stability for use in pervaporation [19,20].

Polyimide has become an important polymer for pervaporation involving organic solvents because of its excellent heat and chemical resistance, strong mechanical strength, and good film-forming properties [21,22]. There are many approaches to improve polyimide performance for pervaporation [21]. As such, the hydrophilicity and packing density of polyimide can be improved through polyimide synthesis using different structures of monomers [23–25], cross-linking of polyimides [19,26,27], surface modifications [28], blending with other polymers [29–31], or embedding fillers [32–36], leading to a high permeation flux without decreasing the selectivity.

Embedding fillers in nanocomposite membranes is one of the effective approaches to enhance the pervaporation efficiency of membranes [32–37]. For example, Xu and Chung [33] embedded UiO-66 into a polyimide in a well-dispersed manner. Because of the increased free volume in the polyimide on account of embedding UiO-66 (20 wt% loading), the water permeability increased to 0.329 mg m−1h−1 kPa−1 while maintaining the mole selectivity (2,209) during the dehydration of isopropanol (feed = 85 wt% aqueous isopropanol at 60 °C). In addition, Kudasheva et al. [34] embedded ZIF-8, ordered mesoporous silica, and ZIF-8-silica core–shell spheres separately into the polyimide matrices. Among these three fillers, the polyimide mixed-matrix membrane containing the ordered mesoporous silica provided the highest performance for the dehydration of water/ethanol mixtures (0.44 kg m−2 h−1 with water/ethanol separation factor of 250; feed = 90 wt% aqueous ethanol solution at 42 °C). It was found that small particles possessed a higher particle-polymer interfacial area that provided better accessibility to silica pores. Apart from that, Hua et al. [36] incorporated ZIF-90 into a polyimide membrane for the dehydration of isopropanol. The incorporation of ZIF-90 with polyethersulfone as primer into polyimide produced a modified membrane with a high selectivity (total flux = 109 g∙m-2h−1; separation factor = 5668; feed = 85 wt% aqueous isopropanol solution at 60 °C).

Recently, carbon-based fillers have shown potential for improving the properties of polymeric membranes [38]. These carbon-based fillers include carbon nanotubes [39,40], graphene and graphene its derivatives [41,42]. Among them, graphene oxide (GO) is the most hydrophilic due to the presence of epoxy, hydroxyl, and carboxylic acid groups [43]. In addition, the functionalization of GO is often utilized to improve its dispersion in organic solvents and compatibility with polymers [32,44–46]. In one robust example, Salehian and Chung [32] functionalized GO with ammonia to improve its compatibility with polyimide. In fact, ammonia-functionalized GO would react with polyimide through amidation reaction. They increased the polyimide performance to 161.5 g∙m-2h−1 with separation factor of >5,000 for dehydration of isopropanol (feed = 85 wt% aqueous isopropanol at 60 °C).

In this study, we synthesized two spirobisindane-containing compounds from bisphenol A (BPA) that would be utilized to functionalize GO to produce spirobisindane-functionalized graphene oxide (SFGO) samples. These SFGO samples would be incorporated respectively into a commercial polyimide, Matrimid® 5218 (M) for pervaporation. Inspired by the spiro-structure from polymers of intrinsic microporosity [47], compounds 3,3,3′,3′-tetramethyl-1,1′-spirobisindane-6,6′-diol (TSD) and 4,4′-((3,3,3′,3′-tetramethyl-2,2′,3,3′-tetrahydro-1,1′-spirobi[indene]-6,6′-diyl)bis(oxy))dianiline (TTSD) were synthesized through a conversion reaction. Both TSD and TTSD compounds exhibited spiro-centers and rigid ring structure that prevented close polymer chain packing. Along with TSD and TTSD, BPA were also chosen for functionalizing GO. The GO samples were respectively functionalized by BPA and TSD through esterification and etherification, whereas another GO sample was functionalized with TTSD through amidation and primary amine-epoxy addition. Each functionalized GO sample was incorporated into the polyimide solution, which was deposited on a polysulfone (PSf) support through spin-coating to produce SFGO@M membranes such as TSD-GO@M and TTSD-GO@M. Embedding different functionalized GO samples in the polyimide matrices would alter the free volume in membranes. In particular, enhanced separation efficiency can be achieved by the polyimide membrane comprising SFGO.

BPA (97+%), as a raw material for the synthesis of spirobisindane derivatives, was bought from Alfa Aesar, Netherlands. Other chemicals used for the synthesis were potassium carbonate (99.5%, Scharlau, Spain), potassium hydroxide (99.9% Scharlau, Spain), palladium on activated carbon (10% Pd, unreduced, Acros USA), 4-fluoronitrobenzene (99.9%, Alfa Aesar, China), methylsulfonic acid (Alfa Aesar, France), hydrazine monohydrate (Alfa Aesar, South Korea), and N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc, greater than99%, Tedia Company Inc., USA). PSf pellets (Udel P-3500) were supplied by Amoco Performance Products, USA. Polyester nonwoven was obtained from Ahlstrom-Munksjö (Helsinki, Finland). Polyethylene glycol (PEG 20 k, MW = 20,000 Da), as an additive to prepare a PSf support, was manufactured by Alfa Aesar, England. Matrimid® 5218 with MW = 80,000 g/mol (99.8%, Alfa Aesar, England) was used as polyimide selective layer. The solvent for PSf and polyimide was N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, 99.5% Tedia Company Inc., USA). n-Propanol, isopropanol, and n-butanol were used as feed in pervaporation experiments, and they were all delivered by Tedia Company Inc., USA with a purity of 99.5%. Dry GO was supplied by Angstrom Materials Inc. (USA). Methanol and ethanol, with purity of 99.5%, were distributed by Echo Chemical Co. Ltd. (Taiwan). Liquid nitrogen and helium were provided by Ming Yang Special Gas Co. Ltd., Taiwan. Celite 545 was provided by Showa Chemical Co. Ltd. (Japan).

Fig. 1 a illustrates the conversion of BPA into spirobisindane derivatives. The synthesis of TSD was similar to the procedure followed by Ma et al. [48]. Accordingly, a reaction flask containing 100 g (0.44 mmol) BPA and 15 mL methanesulfonic acid was heated to 135 °C for 4 h. After the mixture became a burgundy red sticky oil, it was poured into a container containing 1.5 L water under rigorous stirring. Then, it was recrystallized in an ethanol/water (40/60 wt/wt) solution, Greyish yellow powder was obtained, with a 30% yield (47.2 g). 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data are presented in Figure S1 , as follows: 1H NMR (400 MHz, DMSO‑d 6): δ 8.97 (s, 2H), 7.00 (d, J = 8.4 Hz, 2H), 6.59 (dd, J = 8.4 Hz, 2.4 Hz, 2H), 6.10 (d, J = 2.27 Hz, 2H), 2.25 (d, J = 13.02 Hz, 2H), 2.21 (d, J = 13.02 Hz, 2H), 1.31 (s, 6H),1.25 (s, 6H).

TSD was first converted to 3,3,3′,3′-tetramethyl-6,6′-bis(4-nitrophenoxy)-2,2′,3,3′-tetrahydro-1,1′-spirobi[indene] (TBTS). TSD (14.6 g or 1.9 mmol) was mixed in a 250 mL two-neck flask containing 15.31 g (4.3 mmol) 1-fluoro-4-nitrobenzene, 17.99 g K2CO3, and 86.46 mL DMAc. The reaction mixture was kept at room temperature for 4 h. Afterward, it was heated to 150 °C for 12 h. The purification of TBTS was done by precipitation in 50 vol% aqueous ethanol solution. A pale yellow solid was collected after drying in vacuum, with 96.5% yield (27 g). Figure S2 presents 1H NMR (400 MHz, DMSO‑d 6) of TBTS: δ 8.10 (d, J = 9.2 Hz, 4H), 7.34 (d, J = 8.28 Hz, 2H), 7.02 (dd, J = 8.28 Hz, 2.23 Hz, 2H), 6.98 (d, J = 9.2 Hz, 4H), 6.58 (d, J = 2.27 Hz, 2H), 2.42 (d, J = 13.04 Hz, 2H), 2.24 (d, J = 13.04 Hz, 2H), 1.38 (s, 6H), 1.35 (s, 6H).

TBTS was converted to TTSD as follows: 17 g (1 mmol) TBTS and 0.85 g 10% Pd/C were dissolved in 200 mL ethanol with 51 mL hydrazine monohydrate in a 500-mL two-neck flask. The reaction mixture was stirred at 70 ℃ in nitrogen atmosphere for 2 h. Afterward, the hot mixture was filtered using Celite 545, where the catalyst was removed. The filtrate was poured by ethanol to recrystallize the TTSD (white color). The yield was 72.8% (11.04 g). The mass spectrum shows in Figure S3
, MS m/z, calcd. for C33H34N2O2: 490.26; anal.: 491.27. Figure S4 shows the 1H NMR (400 MHz, DMSO‑d 6) of TTSD: δ7.12 (d, J = 8.28 Hz, 2H), 6.70 (dd, J = 8.28 Hz, 2.36 Hz, 2H), 6.65 (d, J = 8.8 Hz, 4H), 6.98 (d, J = 9.2 Hz, 4H), 6.53 (d, J = 8.84 Hz, 4H), 6.18 (d, J = 2.36 Hz, 2H), 4.9 (s, 4H), 2.3 (d, J = 13 Hz, 2H), 2.09 (d, J = 13 Hz, 2H), 1.29 (s, 6H), 1.27 (s, 6H); Figure S5 shows the 13C NMR (125 MHz, DMSO‑d 6) of TTSD: δ158.5, 151.7, 146.4, 145.7, 145.4, 123.2, 120.5, 116.4, 115.1, 111.9, 59.4, 57.4, 42.8, 31.7, 30.5.

Fig. 1b describes the functionalization of GO with BPA, TSD, or TTSD. For example, the BPA (0.5 wt%) was dissolved in NMP for 30 min. Afterward, GO was added to the BPA /NMP solution. The BPA reacted with GO at 95 °C for 24 h. A functionalized GO was obtained by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 10 min. Centrifugation was done three times. The solvent for the first centrifugation was NMP to remove the unreacted BPA. Then, water was used for the second and last centrifugation. Finally, the wet modified GO was freeze-dried for 24 h.

PSf support was prepared in a similar way as in our previous work [49]. PSf and PEG 20 k were dissolved in NMP at 50 °C in an agitating mechanical mixer for 24 h. The concentration of PSf was 18 wt%, and NMP was 82 wt%. PEG 20 k was added as an additive, with a concentration of 50 wt% (based on the amount of PSf). The PSf solution was degassed at 30 °C for 24 h. Afterward, it was cast in a continuous casting machine fed with a polyester nonwoven. The excess NMP was removed by immersing the membrane support in a container filled with water. A roll of PSf support was obtained and stored in a 1 wt% sodium bisulfite (NaHSO3) solution at room temperature.

Fig. 2 illustrates the preparation of a defect-free nanocomposite polyimide membrane. Pieces of PSf support were washed several times with distilled water to remove NaHSO3. Then, they were cut to make round samples with a diameter of 5 cm2, which were ultimately dried overnight. A dry PSf support was placed on a spin-coating machine which was set in motion at 4,500 rpm initially for 10 s, a time enough to establish steady-state conditions. After that, 230 µL of polyimide solution (12 wt% polyimide/NMP) was dropped onto the center of the PSf support using micropipette, and the system was allowed to spin for 45 s. This was the first spin coating. The machine was then left to rotate for 10 s to ensure steady-state conditions at 4,500 rpm, before a second spin coating of another 230 µL of polyimide solution was done in a manner similar to the first spin coating. After two layers of solution were spin-coated onto the support, the resultant membrane was cured at 60 °C for 30 min. Varied rates of spin coating were considered to determine the best spin-coating conditions.

Membranes infused with GO or modified GO were fabricated as follows. First, particles were dispersed in NMP through sonication. Then, polyimide was added to dissolve it in NMP. After that, spin coating of the solution was done in a way similar to the preparation of pristine composite polyimide membrane. The filler concentration was varied from 0 to 1 wt% (based on the amount of polyimide). The membrane without GO was represented by M, whereas that with particles was named X@M, where X referred to GO or modified GO.

NMR spectra of chemical structures in this study were obtained using Bruker AVIII HD 400NMR (Bruker, USA) with DMSO‑d 6 (Sigma-Aldrich, Darmstadt, Germany) as solvent, to verify the structure. The functionalized GOs and membranes were also confirmed using attenuated total reflectance − Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR, PerkinElmer Spectrum 100 FT-IR Spectrometer, USA) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (PS VG K-alpha, ThermoFisherScientific Inc., USA). Particles and membranes were vacuum dried before taped on the sample stage for testing. The membrane morphology was observed using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, S-4800, Hitachi Co., Japan, acceleration voltage = 3 kV). The distribution of N in composite membranes was determined using FESEM installed with energy dispersive X-Ray spectroscopy (EDX, Ultim® Max, Oxford Instruments, High Wycombe, UK). For cross-sectional images, membrane samples were freeze-fractured in liquid nitrogen. For all FESEM samples, platinum was sputtered on surface and cross-section of the membrane at 15 mA for 150 s.

The crystallinity of particles and membranes was characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Model D8 Advance Eco, Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA). The membrane surface hydrophilicity was determined using an automatic interfacial tensiometer (PD-VP Model, Kyowa Interface Science Co. Ltd., Japan). Deionized water was dropped on the sample surface with approximately 5 µL using a micro syringe. Free volume was analyzed using positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS, R&D Center for Membrane Technology, Taiwan).

The dehydration of alcohols was conducted using a pervaporation setup similar to what we used in our previous study [50]. In this setup, two membranes could be tested at the same time. The concentration of feed and permeate (wt%) was determined using gas chromatography (Personal GC1000, China Chromatography Co., Ltd., Taiwan). ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of GO and modified GO
ce:section.ce:para:
Prior to adding GO or modified GO to the polyimide solution, they were characterized using ATR-FTIR, XRD (Fig. 3 ), and XPS (Table S1). Fig. 3a represents the ATR-FTIR spectra of GO, BPA-GO, TSD-GO, and TTSD-GO. Commercial GO had typical peaks at 3275, 1719, 1584, 1409, 1224, and 1046 cm−1, corresponding to hydroxyl (OH), carboxyl (CO), aromatic (CC), carbonyl (COH), epoxy (CO), and alkoxy (CO) groups in GO, respectively [51]. When GO was modified with BPA or TSD, new peaks were observed at 1640 and 1110 cm−1, attributed to ester and ether groups, respectively. Ester groups were formed through esterification of the carboxyl groups of GO with the hydroxyl groups of BPA or TSD, whereas ether groups were formed through etherification of the epoxy groups of GO and the hydroxyl groups of BPA or TSD. On the other hand, amidation and amine-epoxy reactions between TTSD and GO occurred. The new peak for TTSD-GO was located at 1648 (CO), 1475 (CN), and 1211 (CN) cm−1, indicating amide I, II, and III bonds, respectively [52]. Furthermore, according to the XPS analysis (Table S1,
Figure S6 ), the C/O ratio for particles increased in the following order: GO (1.6) < BPA-GO (2.7) < TSD-GO (3.1) < TTSD-GO (5.0). The increasing order was in accordance with the amount of carbon in structures, where the amount of carbon in TTSD > TSD > BPA. C1s and O1s spectra of the GO and modified GO were presented in Figure S7
and
Figure S8 , respectively. The area of the epoxides at peak 286.7 eV in the C1s spectra decreases in the following order: GO > BPA-GO > TSD-GO > TTSD-GO. During the functionalization of GO, its epoxides open its rings and undergo etherification with BPA or TTSD; or amidation with TTSD. Figure S9 presents the N1s spectra of the TTSD-GO. The binding energy of the amine and amide group was overlapping at 399.9 eV. Therefore, the results showed that BPA, TSD, or TTSD was covalently grafted onto GO.

Figure S10 shows the morphology of GO and modified GO. The GO nanosheets had a wrinkled structure and consist of 2–3 overlapping layers. After modification, the BPA-GO, TSD-GO, and TTSD-GO resembles a vivid (black) color, which caused by the intercalating of BPA or TSD or TTSD in the GO nanosheets [53].

Fig. 3b compares the XRD patterns of GO and functionalized GO. GO had a peak at 2Θ = 10.7°, corresponding to a d-spacing of 8.27 Å [54]. When GO was functionalized with BPA, the peak shifted to 8.68°. This means that BPA intercalated with GO sheets, resulting in increased d-spacing, from 8.27 to 10.19 Å. For TSD-GO, two peaks were observed at 6.81 and 9.30°, corresponding to d-spacings equal to 12.98 and 9.51 Å, respectively. These two peaks indicated that the second hydroxyl group in TSD probably did not react with the carboxyl or epoxy group in GO. If this happened, the hydroxyl group could form a hydrogen bond with unreacted oxygen functional groups or with other hydroxyl groups in TSD within TSD-GO, resulting in two different interlayer spacings in TSD-GO. TTSD-GO had the largest d-spacing of 14.32 Å (6.17°), because among the functionalized GO, TTSD had the longest group between terminal amines. Hence, BPA-GO and SFGO samples was successfully developed.

The deposition of a thin layer of polyimide on polyester nonwoven through spin coating would result in nonuniform and unstable membranes for pervaporation. To deposit a thin layer of polyimide, the polymer solution should have a suitable concentration and viscosity. Table 1 lists the performance of composite polyimide membranes with either polyester nonwoven or PSf as support. Although 2 layers of polyimide had been spin-coated on polyester nonwoven, overflow was inevitable during the pervaporation test. However, in the case of spin-coating 2 layers of polyimide on PSf, a high separation performance was achieved during the dehydration of 70 wt% aqueous isopropanol solution, where the permeation flux = 619.3 ± 124.0 g∙m-2h−1 and the water concentration in the permeate = 97.27 ± 2.21 wt%. Therefore, PSf support helped polyimide to form a dense matrix with 2-time deposition.

In spin-coating processes, the number of times of depositing the polymer solution on the membrane surface and the spinning rate would both affect the membrane morphology, active layer thickness, and performance of composite membranes. Fig. 4 indicates the performance of M membranes with variable spin-coated layers and those produced from varied spinning rates. The number of spin-coated layers was varied from 1 to 4 (Fig. 4a). One-time spin coating was insufficient to fabricate a dense polyimide layer ( Figure S12 ). During the spin-coating process, part of PSf was also dissolved, and the remaining part blended with polyimide, as can be deduced from the cross-sectional images in Figure S12 . That is why a dense polyimide layer was not formed (with one-time spin coating), and the resultant membrane turned out defective for dehydrating isopropanol. Increasing the number of spin-coated layers from 2 to 4 decreased the permeation flux from 619.3 ± 124.0 to 531.7 ± 76.1 g∙m-2h−1, because the polyimide/PSf matrix thickness increased from 24.20 ± 2.13 to 35.28 ± 3.89 μm, leading to an increase of mass transfer resistance. Nonetheless, the water concentration in the permeate was maintained from 94.81 ± 2.31 to 97.27 ± 2.21 wt%.

Another factor in spin coating is the spinning rate (Fig. 4b). In general, the faster the spinning rate, the thinner the coating layer [55–57]. Increasing the spinning rate from 2,500 to 6,500 rpm decreased the membrane thickness from 35.57 ± 2.35 to 23.35 ± 2.25 μm, which resulting in raise of permeation flux from 545.5 ± 49.3 to 952.5 ± 177.7 g∙m-2h−1. However, the water concentration in the permeate decreased from 98.82 ± 1.19 to 88.52 ± 13.49 wt%. Decreased selectivity at high spinning rates might be attributed to the inability of layers to form well, despite two layers of polyimide were deposited on the composite membrane, as demonstrated by FESEM images in Figure S13 . Therefore, the subsequent section considers the deposition of two layers of polyimide on the composite membrane at a spinning rate of 4,500 rpm.

Asymmetric and symmetric SO stretching of PSf support was located at 1327–1293 and 1178–1147 cm−1 (Fig. 5
a) [49]. When polyimide was spin-coated on the PSf support twice, strong new peaks for polyimide emerged at 1778 (CO symmetric stretch), 1717 (CO asymmetric stretch), 1365 (CN stretch), and 1088 cm−1 (CN stretch) [58,59]. CNC of polyimide overlapped with the PSf support at 1086 cm−1. However, incorporating GO or modified GO into nanocomposite polyimide membranes made no significant change, as indicated in the ATR-FTIR spectra, because the amount of GO or modified GO was too little that ATR-FTIR could not detect it. According to the EDX mapping of the N element, the dense polyimide layer thickness could be estimated to be 9 µm (Fig. 5 b). Therefore, spin coating of polyimide on the PSf support enabled the deposition of a thin and dense selective polyimide layer.

Incorporating GO into the matrix of polyimide could result in increased free volume in the overall membrane. Fig. 7 describes PALS analysis for nanocomposite membranes, which was reported in terms of data on S parameter vs. positron incident energy. The larger the S parameter, the larger the free volume. There was a sudden drop in S parameter at positron incident energies less than 0.8 keV. These sudden drops happened when positrons are closer to the sample surface. The defects and different chemical nature of the surface can be detected. Furthermore, this was also probably due to the behavior of positron at high vacuum within the cavity. At less than 18 keV, a plateau region of S parameter was observed. At more than 18 keV, there was an increase in S parameter, and this was possibly from the interface between the PSf support and the polyimide matrix.

The free volume in membranes increased in the following order: M < GO@M < BPA-GO@M < SFGO@M because SFGO compounds exhibited spirobisindane structure that prevented close polymer chain packing. From the comparison of SFGO@M samples, TTSD-GO@M sample had the largest free volume. This is probably because incorporating TTSD-GO with larger structure into the polyimide matrix led to the creation of large free volume at the interface between polyimide chains and TTSD-GO. Furthermore, TTSD-GO had the highest d-spacing (Fig. 3b), when added in the membrane, it can also affect the total free volume of the membrane.

On the other hand, GO@M membrane had lower free volume than the other modified membranes, because GO and polyimide had strong interaction with each other through hydrogen bonding, which could lead to a more compact membrane. GO also had the lowest d-spacing (Fig. 3b), when embedded in the membrane, the free volume might not be that high. Furthermore, unmodified GO only had the small molecules of hydroxyl and epoxy groups on its structure. Consequently, when GO was incorporated into the polyimide matrix, the free volume between them could also be small. Therefore, embedding SFGO enlarged the free volume of the polyimide matrix.

In pervaporation, hydrophilicity, free volume, and thickness of membranes, all affect the membrane performance. Fig. 8 shows the performance of composite membranes. All composite membranes had a water concentration in the permeate from 97 to 99 wt%, indicating that embedding GO or modified GO in polyimide had insignificant effect on the water concentration in the permeate. M, GO@M, and BPA-GO@M membranes had similar permeation flux from 619.3 to 664.3 g∙m-2h−1. When each of TSD-GO and TTSD-GO was embedded in the membrane, the permeation flux increased to 816.8 ± 12.5 g∙m-2h-1and 915.5 ± 44.8 g∙m-2h−1, respectively. When SFGO was incorporated into polyimide, free volume in the overall membrane turned out to be also large. Hence, TTSD-GO@M had the highest permeation flux. Because the membrane hydrophilicity and thickness for unmodified and modified membranes were similar, the increment in permeation flux during pervaporation was probably because of the large free volume, which is supported by PALS analysis (Fig. 7).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of GO and modified GO concentrations
ce:section.ce:para: Different particles added to the polymeric matrix require different optimal concentrations. Fig. 9 plots the membrane performance vs the concentration of particles from 0 to 1 wt%. For the case of using GO and BPA-GO (Fig. 9a and b), the membrane performance remained the same with increasing particle concentrations. This is probably because GO could also act as a barrier during pervaporation. The interfacial free volume between GO or BPA-GO and polyimide compromised the mass transfer resistance. Although the free volume was increased after modification, the GO acts as a barrier that could increase the mass transfer resistance of the membrane. Hence, the permeation flux and water concentration in the permeate remained approximately 600 g∙m-2h−1 and 97–99 wt%, respectively.

Optimum membrane performance of SFGO samples were attained (Fig. 9c and d). For TSD-GO@M, the optimum concentration of TSD-GO was 0.1 wt%, where permeation flux = 893.0 ± 114.4 g∙m-2h−1 and water concentration in the permeate = 98.56 ± 1.78 wt% (β = 158). Compared with TSD-GO@M, TTSD-GO@M had optimum performance at 0.5 wt% TTSD-GO, where permeation flux = 915.5 ± 44.8 g∙m-2h−1 and water concentration in the permeate = 99.17 ± 0.56 wt% (β = 279). TTSD-GO@M had a higher d-spacing and larger free volume than TSD-GO@M (Fig. 6a and Fig. 7), thus TTSD-GO@M had the higher permeation flux. Therefore, polyimide membrane containing GO modified with larger spirobisindane structure (TTSD-GO@M) would result in higher permeation flux.

Fig. 10 reports the TTSD-GO@M membrane performance at different feed temperatures and isopropanol concentrations in the feed. Increasing the feed temperature from 25 to 70 °C increased the permeation flux from 915.5 to 993 g∙m-2h−1, with the water concentration in the permeate greater than 95 wt%. At high temperature, the mobility of water molecules increased thereby increasing the permeation flux as well. In addition, a movement of the polymeric segments at high temperature could lead to an increase in free volume, which facilitates the enhancement of permeation flux across the membrane. Furthermore, at high temperature, the vapour pressure difference of permeating molecules created across the membrane also increased, resulting in an increase of permeation flux.

The amount of alcohol in the feed also affected the membrane performance (Fig. 10b). Increasing the isopropanol concentration from 10 to 90 wt% increased the permeation flux from 773.4 to 1,047.3 g∙m-2h−1. Polyimide had a strong affinity with isopropanol. At high isopropanol concentrations, therefore, the membrane was swollen, and isopropanol was then trapped within polyimide chains, and this led to high permeation flux. Nevertheless, the water concentration in the permeate was maintained greater than 93 wt%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Pervaporation separation for different alcohol-water mixtures
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 11 presents the performance of TTSD-GO@M membrane tested on different alcohol-water mixtures. Table S2 lists the kinetic diameter of the water and alcohols. All the molecules have lower kinetic diameter than the d-spacing of the TTSD-GO@M membrane. Thus, the interaction of the molecules with the material dominates the separation performance, which follows the solution-diffusion model. The feed concentration was constant at 70 wt% aqueous alcohol solution. TTSD-GO@M gave the following data on permeation flux and water concentration in permeate for different feed alcohols: for methanol feed, flux = 669.1 ± 52.5 g∙m-2h−1 and water concentration = 89.46 ± 1.64 wt%; ethanol, 712.8 ± 61.7 g∙m-2h−1 and 97.30 ± 1.76 wt%; n-propanol, 867.5 ± 41.0 g∙m-2h−1 and 99.71 ± 0.38 wt%; isopropanol, 900.8 ± 24.8 g∙m-2h−1 and 99.17 ± 0.56 wt%; n-butanol, 808.8 ± 21.0 g∙m-2h−1 and 97.70 ± 1.56 wt%. The performance of TTSD-GO@M which was tested on methanol was the lowest because it had the smallest molar volume and kinetic diameter (Table S2), suggesting that methanol could easily penetrate through the membrane. However, when the feed was n-Butanol, the permeation flux of TTSD-GO@M membrane had lower flux than when the feed was n-Propanol or Isopropanol. This was probably because the solubility parameter difference between n-Butanol and the polyimide (Matrimid®) has the lowest value (Table S2). Low solubility parameter difference of the n-Butanol and M membrane indicates that their interaction is strong. During pervaporation process, n-Butanol could have strong interaction with Matrimid®, and could block the water molecules from passing through the membrane, resulting in low permeation flux. Nevertheless, TTSD-GO@M membrane had a high separation performance when it was tested on ethanol, n-propanol, isopropanol, and n-butanol, indicating that it is promising for biofuel separation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Membrane stability test and comparison of membrane performance
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 12 presents long-term stability tests of TTSD-GO@M for 168 h. The permeation flux and water concentration in the permeate remained high, indicating that the membranes could be subjected to long periods of pervaporation operations. Table 2 summarizes the performance for isopropanol dehydration reported by our study and in the literature. Most polyimide membranes reported in the literature were prepared by casting on glass plates. Compared with the polyimide membranes in the literature, our TTSD-GO@M still had the highest permeation flux and had similar water concentration in the permeate. However, the polyimides (P84; Matrimid; Torlon) in literature were cast as free-standing membranes with permeation flux ranging from 8.2 to 161 g∙m-2h−1 with more than 99 wt% water concentration in permeate. This indicates that spin coating of polyimide on a PSf support could give a thin, dense, and defect-free selective polyimide layer. Thinner selective layer facilitates lower mass transfer resistance. Embedding SFGO (especially TTSD-GO) creates larger free volume and water channel, thereby enhancing water permeation flux. Compared with other thin-film composite membranes, TTSD-GO@M still had comparable performance. Those thin-film composite membranes were fabricated through interfacial polymerization, pressure-assisted filtration, casting or dip-coating.

Defect-free membranes for dehydration of alcohols through pervaporation are fabricated by spin coating a thin selective layer of SFGO/polyimide onto the PSf support. The properties and performance of nanocomposite membranes can be enhanced significantly by incorporating the SFGO nanocomposites. Among these nanocomposite membranes, the TTSD-GO@M membrane delivers the highest permeation flux (915.5 ± 44.8 g∙m-2h−1) owing to the large free volume in the polymer matrix. It is important to note that the TTSD-GO@M membrane is also capable of separating various alcohol-water mixtures. Furthermore, this membrane could maintain its stability at 25 °C for a long-term operation (168 h). Therefore, SFGO@M membrane exhibits great potential for applications in biofuel production via effective separation.
